10.1111/apt.12913.results_passage: Four trials met the inclusion criteria, one in constipation and three in non-constipated subjects. In constipation, 3 weeks of prune consumption (100 g/day) improved stool frequency (3.5 vs. 2.8 CSBM per week, P = 0.006) and stool consistency (3.2 vs. 2.8 on Bristol stool form scale, P = 0.02) compared with psyllium (22 g/day). In non-constipated subjects, prunes softened stool consistency in one trial and increased stool weight (628 g vs. 514 g/72 h wet weight, P = 0.001) in another trial, compared with control. In constipation, prunes appear superior to psyllium for improving stool frequency and consistency, however, the evidence for other outcomes and the effects in non-constipated subjects is weak.

10.6133/apjcn.2015.24.3.15.results_passage: There was no difference in total bowel movements over 3 weeks (p>0.05) or mean bowel movements during each of weeks 1, 2 and 3 (p>0.05) between the kiwifruit extract and placebo when assessed from a faecal diary. There was also no detectable difference in defecation related scores of ease of defecation, volume, consistency or stool type assessed using Bristol stool chart scores. Nor was there a significant change in gastrointestinal symptoms rating scale or quality of life between pre and post treatment measures, compared to placebo (p>0.05). This trial showed that improvement in bowel function or comfort was not achieved through supplementation with 1 g/day freeze dried kiwifruit extract.

10.1097/MCG.0b013e3182a88357.results_passage: Nine studies that evaluated 726 patients were identified. Peppermint oil was found to be significantly superior to placebo for global improvement of IBS symptoms (5 studies, 392 patients, relative risk 2.23; 95% confidence interval, 1.78-2.81) and improvement in abdominal pain (5 studies, 357 patients, relative risk 2.14; 95% confidence interval, 1.64-2.79). Although peppermint oil patients were significantly more likely to experience an adverse event, such events were mild and transient in nature. Peppermint oil is a safe and effective short-term treatment for IBS.

10.1016/j.clnesp.2024.02.025.results_passage: A total of 20 studies involving 3011 patients were obtained. The results demonstrated that probiotics are more effective than placebo in reducing global IBS symptoms improvement rate (RR = 1.401, 95% CI 1.182-1.662, P < 0.001) and quality of life scores (SMD = 0.286, 95% CI = 0.154-0.418, P < 0.001). High doses (daily dose of probiotics >= 10^10) or multiple strains of probiotics exhibit beneficial effects on abdominal pain. Probiotics are effective and safe for IBS patients, though high heterogeneity makes definite conclusions challenging.

10.1016/j.nut.2017.07.004.results_passage: Nine RCTs with a total of 596 subjects were included. A meta-analysis revealed significant group differences for the low FODMAP diet compared with other diets with regard to gastrointestinal symptoms (SMD = -0.62; 95% CI = -0.93 to -0.31; P = 0.0001), abdominal pain (SMD = -0.50; 95% CI = -0.77 to -0.22; P = 0.008), and health-related quality of life (SMD = 0.36; 95% CI = 0.10-0.62; P = 0.007). This meta-analysis found evidence of the short-term efficacy and safety of the low FODMAP diet in patients with IBS, though only a preliminary recommendation can be made until long-term effects are investigated.

10.1055/s-2008-1038600.results_passage: Analyses revealed no differences in quality of life scores between groups at 12-week follow-up. The exercise group reported significantly improved symptoms of constipation (mean difference=10.9, 95% CI= -20.1, -1.6) compared to usual care at follow-up. The intervention group participated in significantly more exercise than usual care at follow-up (mean difference=21.6, 95% CI=9.4, 33.8). Findings highlight the possibility that exercise may be an effective intervention for symptom management in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, particularly for constipation predominant patients.

10.1159/000050681.results_passage: The available data clearly demonstrate that inhibition of gastric emptying and stimulation of colonic transit is the most consistent pattern in the motility response of the gastrointestinal tract to acute or short-term stress. The colonic motor response to stress is exaggerated in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), with an increased emotional response associated with this difference in colonic and gastric motor responses to certain stressors. Endogenous corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) in the brain plays a significant role in mediating stress-induced inhibition of upper GI and stimulation of lower GI motor function. Stress-induced activation of mucosal mast cells in the GI tract also appears to be involved in stress-associated alterations of visceral sensitivity.

10.1038/ajg.2016.503.results_passage: A total of 101 adolescents with IBS (13-17 years of age) were included in this study, with low dropout rates (6%). Analyses showed a significantly larger pretreatment to posttreatment change on the primary outcome, Gastrointestinal Symptoms Rating Scale for IBS (B=-6.42, P=0.006, effect size Cohen's d=0.45, 95% CI 0.12-0.77), for the Internet-delivered CBT group compared with the wait-list control group. After 6 months, the results were stable or significantly improved. Internet-delivered CBT based on exposure exercises for adolescents with IBS can effectively improve gastrointestinal symptoms and quality of life.

10.1097/00042737-199802000-00003.results_passage: Caffeinated coffee, decaffeinated coffee and a meal induced more activity in the colon with a greater area under the curve of pressure waves (P < 0.01) and a greater number of propagated contractions (P < 0.05) compared with water. The effects of decaffeinated coffee on colonic motility were not significantly different from those of water or caffeinated coffee, and were lower (P < 0.05) than those of a meal. Caffeinated coffee stimulates colonic motor activity, with a magnitude similar to a meal, 60% stronger than water, and 23% stronger than decaffeinated coffee.

10.1080/13697137.2022.2097865.results_passage: Across 21 RCTs involving 2884 participants, compared to no-treatment control, exercise significantly improved severity of vasomotor symptoms (10 studies, standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.25; 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.47, p = 0.02, very low certainty of evidence); the effect size was attenuated when studies with a high risk of bias were excluded (SMD = 0.11, 95% CI: -0.03 to 0.26, p = 0.13). No significant changes in vasomotor frequency were found between exercise and control (SMD = 0.14, 95% CI: -0.03 to 0.31, p = 0.12, high certainty of evidence). Exercise might improve vasomotor symptom severity, but future rigorous RCTs are warranted to explore optimal exercise prescription.

10.1017/S0033291721005407.results_passage: 14 RCTs comprising 1618 patients with a mean sample size of 116 were included. Cognitive therapy and behavior therapy (CTBT) significantly outperformed control groups in terms of reducing hot flushes (g = 0.39, 95% CI 0.23-0.55), night sweats, depression (g = 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.66), anxiety (g = 0.38, 95% CI 0.23-0.54), fatigue, and quality of life. CTBT is an effective psychological treatment for menopausal symptoms, with predominantly small to moderate effects that are sustained long-term, although the efficacy declines somewhat over time and was stronger for natural menopause symptoms than treatment-induced menopause symptoms.

10.1097/gme.0b013e3182410159.results_passage: From 277 potentially relevant publications, 19 trials were included in the systematic review and 17 trials were selected for meta-analyses. Ingestion of soy isoflavones (median, 54 mg aglycone equivalents) for 6 weeks to 12 months significantly reduced the frequency of hot flashes by 20.6% (95% CI, -28.38 to -12.86; P < 0.00001) compared with placebo. Isoflavones also significantly reduced hot flash severity by 26.2% (95% CI: -42.23 to -10.15, P = 0.001) compared with placebo. Soy isoflavone supplements, derived by extraction or chemical synthesis, are significantly more effective than placebo in reducing the frequency and severity of hot flashes.

10.1177/0022034516655315.results_passage: Of 5,494 titles retrieved, 33 studies were eligible for inclusion. Self-reported infrequent brushers demonstrated higher incidence (odds ratio [OR], 1.50; 95% CI, 1.34 to 1.69) and increment (standardized mean difference [SMD], 0.28; 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44) of carious lesions than frequent brushers. The effect of infrequent brushing on incidence and increment of carious lesions was higher in deciduous (OR: 1.75; 95% CI: 1.49 to 2.06) than permanent dentition (OR: 1.39; 95% CI: 1.29 to 1.49). Meta-regression indicated that none of the included variables (sample size, follow-up period, diagnosis level, methodological quality) influenced the effect estimate.

10.1016/j.amepre.2018.02.014.results_passage: Twenty-eight studies were included in the review; of these, only 14 presented data that could be included in the meta-analysis. Pooled adjusted risk ratios estimate that smoking increases the risk of periodontitis by 85% (risk ratio=1.85, 95% CI=1.5, 2.2). Meta-regression demonstrated that age explained 54.2% of the variability between studies, time of follow-up explained 13.5%, loss to follow-up 10.7%, criteria used to assess periodontal status explained 2.1%, and severity of periodontitis explained 16.9%. Smoking has a detrimental effect on the incidence and progression of periodontitis.

10.1016/S2468-2667(26)00149-0.results_passage: The review screened 45,477 records and included 28 longitudinal studies from 16 countries, encompassing over 300,000 participants. Individuals with periodontitis at baseline showed an 18-25% higher occurrence of newly incident type 2 diabetes during follow-up, and baseline diabetes status was associated with a higher rate of newly incident periodontitis. Tooth loss was also associated with newly incident type 2 diabetes over time (HR 1.12-1.20), and individuals who were edentulous at baseline showed a higher occurrence of newly incident type 2 diabetes (RR 1.30). People with periodontitis and edentulism are more likely to be diagnosed with type 2 diabetes in the future, and people with diabetes are more likely to be diagnosed with periodontitis, though with less consistent evidence.

10.23950/jcmk/15827.results_passage: This systematic review and meta-analysis included six randomised controlled trials published between 2013 and 2020. According to the pooled results of the six studies, calcium reduced the severity of PMS complaints (p=0.002; I2 = 76.2%) when calcium administration was compared with the control group for the reduction of PMS complaints. On the other hand, the severity of PMS complaints did not change when calcium administration was compared with other treatments (p=0.416; I2 = 54.7%). This study showed that calcium effectively reduced the severity of PMS complaints compared to the control groups.

10.1002/art.41416.license: NIH-funded author manuscript (not a CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/art.41416.results_passage: We included 1,398 participants who returned at least one knee pain questionnaire. Mean age was 67.7 years, 66% were female, and mean WOMAC Pain was 37 (SD 19). WOMAC Pain did not differ between vitamin D or marine omega-3 fatty acid supplementation and placebo at any time point during follow-up (linear time by treatment interactions were not statistically significant; vitamin D p=0.41, omega-3 p=0.77). Vitamin D and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for a mean of 5.3 years did not reduce knee pain or improve function or stiffness in a large sample of U.S. adults with chronic knee pain.

10.1186/s13018-023-04182-w.results_passage: Four trials involving 507 patients with knee osteoarthritis were included and analyzed using the random-effects model, though all trials were considered to have a high risk of bias. Results revealed a significant difference in pain relief between the collagen peptide group and the placebo group (standardized mean difference: -0.58; 95% CI -0.98, -0.18, p=0.004; I2: 68%; quality of evidence: moderate). There was no significant difference in the risk of adverse events between collagen peptide and placebo (odds ratio: 1.66; 95% CI 0.99, 2.78, p=0.05). Findings demonstrate significant pain relief in patients with knee osteoarthritis who received collagen peptides compared to placebo, though well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed to validate these findings.

figures.caption: Forest plot demonstrating overall pain scores comparing between collagen peptides and placebo. Better pain control is shown if favor collagen peptides or placebo.
figures.shows: Forest plot of the four included trials showing collagen peptide's pooled standardized mean difference for pain relief versus placebo in knee osteoarthritis.

10.1093/ajcn/nqac184.results_passage: Sixteen RCTs with 1251 participants were included. Overall, 311 of 473 (66%) participants responded to fiber treatment versus 134 of 329 (41%) with control treatment (RR: 1.48; 95% CI: 1.17, 1.88; P=0.001), with psyllium and pectin having significant effects. Fiber increased stool frequency (SMD: 0.72; 95% CI: 0.36, 1.08) and improved stool consistency (SMD: 0.32; 95% CI: 0.18, 0.46), particularly with higher fiber doses (>10 g/d) and treatment durations of at least 4 weeks. Fiber supplementation is effective at improving constipation, though caution is needed when interpreting the results due to considerable heterogeneity.

figures.caption: Forest plot of response to treatment in randomized controlled trials comparing fiber with control groups in adults with chronic constipation (n = 802). Values were calculated as RRs (95% CIs) using a random-effects model. M-H, Mantel-Haenszel; RR, risk ratio.
figures.shows: Forest plot of per-trial risk ratios for responding to fiber supplementation versus control in adults with chronic constipation, pooled across studies.

10.1136/bmj.b3154.results_passage: 275 patients aged 18-65 years with irritable bowel syndrome were randomised to 12 weeks of treatment with psyllium, bran, or placebo. The proportion of responders was significantly greater in the psyllium group than in the placebo group during the first month (57% v 35%; relative risk 1.60, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.26) and the second month of treatment (59% v 41%; 1.44, 1.02 to 2.06). Bran was more effective than placebo during the third month of treatment only (57% v 32%), but this was not statistically significant in the worst case analysis. Psyllium offers benefits in patients with irritable bowel syndrome in primary care.

10.1186/1475-2891-12-78.results_passage: One hundred thirty-eight subjects reporting occasional constipation were screened and 87 were randomized to placebo (n=44) and Kivia powder (n=43). There were significant increases in spontaneous bowel movements (SBM) at week 1 through week 4 compared to baseline, with SBM demonstrating significant differences between treatment and placebo groups at week 3 (p=0.000) and week 4 (p=0.020). Complete spontaneous bowel movements (CSBM) were significantly higher for the treatment group compared to placebo at week 2 (p=0.001), and abdominal discomfort, flatulence, and bowel urgency were also significantly reduced. Treatment with Kivia powder for four weeks was well tolerated and more effective than placebo in enhancing bowel movement frequency and reducing abdominal pain and flatulence in subjects with occasional constipation.

figures.caption: Comparison of Kivia powder and placebo in spontaneous bowel movement. Spontaneous bowel movement was significantly higher for Kivia Powder group compared to placebo group at week 3 and week 4.

10.3390/jcm13164934.results_passage: Eleven studies (n=323) were eligible for the systematic review, of which nine (n=286) were included in the meta-analysis. Pooled analysis revealed a statistically significant decrease in circulating CRP (SMD 0.39, 95% CI 0.22, 0.56), IL-6, TNF-alpha, androstenedione, and luteinising hormone after weight loss compared to baseline levels among PCOS women, alongside a statistically significant increase in circulating SHBG (SMD -0.43, 95% CI -0.65, -0.21). These findings suggest that weight loss induced by dietary interventions seems to improve PCOS-related chronic inflammation and hyperandrogenism, although the causative relationship between the improvement in inflammation and hyperandrogenism remains to be determined.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overall CRP pooled analysis of 9 studies.
figures.shows: Forest plot of the pooled standardized mean difference in circulating CRP before versus after diet-induced weight loss across 9 studies in women with PCOS.

10.1530/EC-17-0243.results_passage: Nine RCTs involving 247 cases and 249 controls were included. Significant decreases in fasting insulin (SMD = -1.021 uU/mL, 95% CI: -1.791 to -0.251, P=0.009) and HOMA index (SMD = -0.585, 95% CI: -1.145 to -0.025, P=0.041) were identified after myo-inositol supplementation. A significant increase in serum SHBG was observed only in studies where myo-inositol was administered for at least 24 weeks (SMD = 0.425 nmol/L, 95% CI: 0.050-0.801, P=0.026). These results highlight the beneficial effect of myo-inositol in improving the metabolic profile of women with PCOS, concomitantly reducing their hyperandrogenism.

10.1038/s41598-018-34303-z.results_passage: Six RCTs met the inclusion criteria. Two RCTs found favorable effects of heat therapy on menstrual pain compared with unheated placebo therapy, three RCTs found favorable effects of heating pads on menstrual pain compared with analgesic medication (n=274; SMD -0.72; 95% CI -0.97 to -0.48; P<0.001), and one RCT showed beneficial effects of heat therapy compared with no treatment (n=132; MD -4.04 VAS; 95% CI -4.88 to -3.20; P<0.001). This review provided suggestive evidence of the effectiveness of heat therapy for primary dysmenorrhea, but rigorous high-quality trials with larger sample sizes are still needed to provide robust evidence.

figures.caption: Forest plot of the heat therapy and control.
figures.shows: Forest plot of pooled effect estimates for menstrual pain reduction comparing heat therapy against control/placebo/analgesic comparators across the included RCTs.

10.1136/bmj.318.7195.1375.license: Copyright BMJ 1999 (pre-CC era, no open license; not reusable)
10.1136/bmj.318.7195.1375.results_passage: Nine published trials representing 940 patients with premenstrual syndrome were included. The odds ratio relative to placebo for an improvement in overall premenstrual symptoms was 2.32 (95% CI 1.95 to 2.54), and the odds ratio for improvement in depressive symptoms was 1.69 (1.39 to 2.06) from four trials representing 541 patients. Conclusions are limited by the low quality of most of the trials included. Results suggest that doses of vitamin B-6 up to 100 mg/day are likely to be of benefit in treating premenstrual symptoms and premenstrual depression, but a randomised controlled trial of sufficient power and quality is needed to establish definitive recommendations.

10.1016/j.ajog.2019.10.103.license: NIH-funded author manuscript (not a CC license; not reusable)
10.1016/j.ajog.2019.10.103.results_passage: Pooled data on 21,460 midlife women from eight studies were used for cross-sectional analysis, with four studies providing prospective data (n=11,986). Never smokers who were obese had a 1.5-fold (RRR 1.52; 95% CI 1.35-1.73) higher risk of often/severe vasomotor symptoms compared with never smokers of normal weight, and the risk was much greater among smokers who were obese (RRR 3.02; 95% CI 2.41-3.78). Smokers who quit before age 40 were at similar risk levels as never smokers, and higher body mass index was associated with increased risk of vasomotor symptoms in pre- and perimenopause but with reduced risk postmenopause. High body mass index and cigarette smoking substantially increased women's risk of frequent or severe vasomotor symptoms in a dose-response manner, and maintaining normal weight and quitting smoking before age 40 may mitigate this excess risk.

10.1016/j.heliyon.2021.e08338.results_passage: Of 935 initial publications, 8 articles were finally included, covering 412 overweight and obese individuals with PCOS. Measured emotional health (3 studies, 132 participants, SMD: -1.97; 95% CI -3.54, -0.40, P=0.01) and body hair (3 studies, 132 participants, SMD: -0.40; 95% CI -0.46, -0.35, P<0.0001) were significantly lower in women on a low glycemic index diet (LGD) versus control diet groups, while infertility (SMD: 1.45; 95% CI 0.30, 2.61, P=0.01) was significantly higher in the LGD group. The meta-analysis shows LGD may play a significant role in reducing risk and improving clinical and biochemical features of PCOS, though evidence is not yet strong enough for a definite dietary recommendation.

10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e14291.results_passage: 13 RCTs with 840 PCOS patients were included. Meta-analyses indicated that vitamin D supplementation increased serum vitamin D level (MD=17.81, 95% CI 10.65, 24.97) and endometrial thickness (MD=1.78, 95% CI 0.49, 3.06, P=0.007), and reduced serum hs-CRP, parathyroid hormone, total cholesterol, and total testosterone level (all P<0.05). No significant differences in SHBG level or modified Ferriman-Gallwey score between vitamin D and control groups were found. Vitamin D may be helpful to improve endocrine and metabolism-related indexes in patients with PCOS, though more high-quality studies with larger sample sizes are warranted.

10.1177/0022034513508954.license: No CC license found (publisher copyright; not reusable)
10.1177/0022034513508954.results_passage: From 5,990 papers identified, 55 studies were eligible: 3 intervention, 8 cohort, 20 population, and 24 cross-sectional studies. Of these, 42 of 50 studies in children and 5 of 5 in adults reported at least one positive association between sugars intake and caries. There is evidence of moderate quality showing that caries is lower when free-sugars intake is less than 10% of energy; with a less-than-5%-of-energy cut-off, a significant relationship was observed, but the evidence was judged to be of very low quality. Data variability limited meta-analysis, but the findings are relevant to minimizing caries risk throughout the life course.

10.1002/14651858.CD003053.pub6.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD003053.pub6.results_passage: 48 studies (4451 women) were included, 42 of which investigated metformin (4024 women); evidence quality ranged from very low to moderate. Metformin may improve live birth rates compared with placebo (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.51, 4 studies, 435 women, low-quality evidence), and had higher rates of clinical pregnancy (OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.42 to 2.64) and ovulation (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.81 to 3.59), though the metformin group experienced more gastrointestinal side effects (OR 4.76, 95% CI 3.06 to 7.41). An improvement in clinical pregnancy and ovulation suggests that clomiphene citrate remains preferable to metformin for ovulation induction in obese women with PCOS, while combined metformin and clomiphene citrate therapy may be useful, although it is unclear whether this translates into increased live births.

10.1002/14651858.CD001751.pub3.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD001751.pub3.results_passage: 80 randomised controlled trials (5820 women) comparing 20 different NSAIDs versus placebo, paracetamol or each other were included. Among women with primary dysmenorrhoea, NSAIDs were more effective for pain relief than placebo (OR 4.37, 95% CI 3.76 to 5.09; 35 RCTs, low quality evidence), meaning that if 18% of women taking placebo achieve moderate or excellent pain relief, between 45% and 53% taking NSAIDs will do so. However, NSAIDs were associated with more adverse effects (overall adverse effects OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.51; gastrointestinal adverse effects OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.23). NSAIDs appear to be a very effective treatment for dysmenorrhoea, though women using them need to be aware of the substantial risk of adverse effects, and there is insufficient evidence to determine which individual NSAID is safest and most effective.

10.1002/14651858.CD004142.pub4.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD004142.pub4.results_passage: 12 trials with 854 women were included in the review, with 10 trials and 754 women in the meta-analysis; nine compared exercise with no treatment and one compared exercise with NSAIDs. Exercise may have a large effect on reducing menstrual pain intensity compared to no exercise (standardised mean difference -1.86, 95% CI -2.06 to -1.66; 9 RCTs, n=632, low-quality evidence), corresponding to a 25mm reduction on a 100mm visual analogue scale that is likely clinically significant. The current low-quality evidence suggests that exercise, performed for about 45 to 60 minutes each time, three times per week or more, regardless of intensity, may provide a clinically significant reduction in menstrual pain intensity. Given the overall health benefits of exercise and its relatively low risk of side effects, women may consider using exercise, alone or with NSAIDs, to manage menstrual pain, though further research using validated outcome measures is required.

10.1002/14651858.CD007244.pub2.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD007244.pub2.results_passage: Sixteen randomised controlled trials recruiting a total of 2027 perimenopausal or postmenopausal women were identified, using oral monopreparations of black cohosh at a median daily dose of 40mg for a mean duration of 23 weeks. There was no significant difference between black cohosh and placebo in the frequency of hot flushes (mean difference 0.07 flushes per day; 95% CI -0.43 to 0.56; 393 women; three trials) or in menopausal symptom scores. Compared to black cohosh, hormone therapy significantly reduced daily hot flush frequency and menopausal symptom scores (SMD 0.32; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.51; 468 women; five trials). There is currently insufficient evidence to support the use of black cohosh for menopausal symptoms, though there is adequate justification for conducting further studies in this area.

10.1002/14651858.CD007868.pub3.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD007868.pub3.results_passage: 96 studies published between 1955 and 2014 were included in this updated review, covering fluoride toothpaste concentrations from 1500 ppm down through lower concentrations across primary and permanent dentition. In the primary dentition of young children, 1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste reduces caries increment when compared with non-fluoride toothpaste (mean difference -1.86 dfs, 95% CI -2.51 to -1.21; moderate-certainty evidence), and toothbrushing with 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste slightly reduces decayed/missing/filled teeth increment compared with 440 ppm fluoride toothpaste. A dose-response effect was observed for D(M)FS in children and adolescents across the network meta-analysis. This review supports the benefits of using fluoride toothpaste in preventing caries compared to non-fluoride toothpaste, though evidence for the effects of different fluoride concentrations is more limited and the choice of concentration for young children should be balanced against the risk of fluorosis.

10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3.results_passage: Fifty-six trials met the inclusion criteria; 51 trials involving 4624 participants provided data for meta-analysis. There is moderate quality evidence that powered toothbrushes provide a statistically significant benefit compared with manual toothbrushes for reduction of plaque in both the short term (SMD -0.50, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.31; 40 trials, n=2871) and long term (SMD -0.47, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.11; 14 trials, n=978), corresponding to an 11% and 21% reduction in plaque respectively. Powered toothbrushes also provide a statistically significant benefit for gingivitis in the short term (SMD -0.43, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.25) and long term (SMD -0.21, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.12). Powered toothbrushes reduce plaque and gingivitis more than manual toothbrushing in the short and long term, although the clinical importance of these findings remains unclear.

10.1002/14651858.CD012018.pub2.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD012018.pub2.results_passage: 35 RCTs (3929 randomised adult participants) were included, evaluating interdental devices such as floss, interdental brushes, wooden cleaning sticks, rubber/elastomeric cleaning sticks, and oral irrigators plus toothbrushing versus toothbrushing alone. Low-certainty evidence suggested that flossing, in addition to toothbrushing, may reduce gingivitis (measured by gingival index) at one month (SMD -0.58, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.04; 8 trials, 585 participants). Very low-certainty evidence suggested that using an interdental brush, plus toothbrushing, may reduce gingivitis at one month (MD -0.53, 95% CI -0.83 to -0.23; 1 trial, 62 participants). Using floss or interdental brushes in addition to toothbrushing may reduce gingivitis or plaque more than toothbrushing alone, and interdental brushes may be more effective than floss, though overall the evidence was low to very low-certainty.

10.1002/14651858.CD008676.pub2.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD008676.pub2.results_passage: 51 studies analysing a total of 5345 participants were included. After 4 to 6 weeks of use, chlorhexidine mouthrinse reduced gingivitis by 0.21 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.31) compared to placebo, control or no mouthrinse (10 trials, 805 participants with mild gingival inflammation, high-quality evidence), with a similar effect at 6 months. Plaque was reduced by a standardized mean difference of 1.45 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.90) standard deviations in the chlorhexidine group (12 trials, 950 participants, high-quality evidence), a large reduction, but there was also a large increase in extrinsic tooth staining (SMD 1.07, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.34). There is high-quality evidence of a large reduction in dental plaque and a reduction in gingivitis (not considered clinically relevant in mildly inflamed gingivae) with chlorhexidine mouthrinse used as an adjunct to mechanical oral hygiene procedures, but rinsing for 4 weeks or longer causes extrinsic tooth staining and other adverse effects.

10.1002/14651858.CD010743.pub2.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD010743.pub2.results_passage: 10 studies analysing a total of 5903 participants were included. Over 2.5 to 3 years of use, a fluoride toothpaste containing 10% xylitol may reduce caries by 13% compared to a fluoride-only toothpaste (prevented fraction -0.13, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.08, 4216 children analysed, low-quality evidence). One study reported that xylitol syrup (8 g per day) reduced caries by 58% (95% CI 33% to 83%, 94 infants) compared to a low-dose xylitol syrup. There is some low-quality evidence to suggest that fluoride toothpaste containing xylitol may be more effective than fluoride-only toothpaste for preventing caries in the permanent teeth of children, but the remaining evidence on other xylitol-containing products is of low to very low quality and insufficient to determine a benefit in infants, older children, or adults.

10.1002/14651858.CD004625.pub5.license: Cochrane copyright (not a reuse-permitting CC license; not reusable)
10.1002/14651858.CD004625.pub5.results_passage: Two studies with 1711 participants, conducted in UK general dental practices among adults without severe periodontitis, were included. There was little or no difference between routine scale-and-polish treatment and no scheduled treatment over a two- to three-year period for gingivitis, probing depths, and oral health-related quality of life (all high-certainty evidence), and for plaque (low-certainty evidence). Regular planned scale-and-polish treatments produced a small reduction in calculus levels over two to three years compared with no scheduled treatment (high-certainty evidence), with six-monthly treatments reducing calculus more than 12-monthly treatments, though the clinical importance of these small reductions is uncertain. For adults without severe periodontitis who regularly access routine dental care, routine scale-and-polish treatment makes little or no difference to gingivitis, probing depths, and oral health-related quality of life.

goals.name: Inflammation / skin
goals.definition: Systemic low-grade inflammation (hs-CRP, IL-6) and skin outcomes (acne severity, sebum production), with insulin/IGF-1 as the mechanistic link between diet and acne.

goals.name: Sleep quality
goals.definition: Composite of circadian alignment (melatonin phase / DLMO), sleep continuity (onset latency), sleep architecture (slow-wave and REM proportion), and subjective sleep quality (PSQI/ISI).

goals.name: Cardiometabolic health
goals.definition: Blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, HbA1c/fasting glucose, insulin sensitivity (HOMA-IR), cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max), and resting heart rate / arterial stiffness (pulse wave velocity) as measurable markers of cardiovascular and metabolic disease risk.

goals.name: Body composition and strength
goals.definition: Fat mass / body fat percentage, fat-free (lean) mass, maximal strength (1RM), waist circumference / visceral adipose tissue, and resting metabolic rate, as driven by resistance training, diet composition and structure, sleep, alcohol, and pharmacology (GLP-1 receptor agonists).

goals.name: Cognition and focus
goals.definition: Working memory, sustained attention/reaction time, episodic memory, global cognition (MMSE/MoCA) in older adults, and processing speed, each tied to a named instrument or task rather than a composite or mortality-style outcome.

goals.name: Mood and anxiety
goals.definition: Depressive symptom severity (PHQ-9, BDI, HAM-D), anxiety symptom severity (GAD-7, STAI, HAM-A, BAI), perceived stress (PSS), and cortisol (salivary, diurnal slope) as the mechanistic stress-axis link. Named-instrument evidence only; mortality and quality-of-life-years outcomes are out of scope.

goals.name: Longevity and mortality risk
goals.definition: Risk of death from any cause (all-cause mortality), death from cardiovascular disease (cardiovascular mortality), and cancer occurrence or death (cancer incidence/mortality), each reported as hazard ratios or relative risks from the literature. This goal is one of eight in the explorer and is not a common unit that other goals' outcomes are converted into; no other goal's endpoints are re-expressed in mortality terms here, and no life-expectancy-years figures are computed from hazard ratios.

goals.name: Liver health
goals.definition: Liver fat content (hepatic steatosis), liver enzymes (ALT/AST), liver stiffness/fibrosis stage, and hepatic insulin sensitivity as measurable markers of non-alcoholic and alcohol-related fatty liver disease risk and progression.

goals.name: Immune function and infection resistance
goals.definition: Acute respiratory tract infection incidence, infection duration/symptom-day count, vaccine antibody response (seroconversion/titre), and experimental infection susceptibility as measurable markers of immune competence against common infections.

goals.name: Bone and joint health
goals.definition: Bone mineral density (site-specific: lumbar spine, femoral neck, total hip), fracture incidence, and knee/hip osteoarthritis pain and physical function, as driven by resistance and impact exercise, protein, calcium and vitamin D intake, smoking, alcohol, body weight, sedentary time, collagen peptides, glucosamine/chondroitin, and omega-3.

goals.name: Gut and digestive health
goals.definition: Stool frequency and consistency, IBS symptom severity, whole-gut/colonic transit time, and constipation responder rate as measurable markers of lower-GI function, using hard endpoints rather than microbiome composition.

goals.name: Oral health
goals.definition: Dental caries increment (DMFS/DMFT increment or prevented fraction), gingival inflammation (gingival or bleeding index), periodontal probing depth / clinical attachment level, and dental plaque (plaque index) as measurable markers of tooth decay and periodontal disease risk.

goals.name: Male vitality / testosterone
goals.definition: Composite goal spanning serum testosterone, vascular/erectile function, lean mass and strength, and subjective libido in adult men.

goals.name: Female reproductive and hormonal health
goals.definition: Menopausal vasomotor symptom frequency or severity, menstrual pain (dysmenorrhoea), premenstrual symptom severity (PMS), PCOS-related hyperandrogenism (total/free testosterone, androstenedione, Ferriman-Gallwey hirsutism score), and menstrual cyclicity or ovulation rate as the markers. Named-instrument or biochemical/clinical-marker evidence only; mortality and quality-of-life-years outcomes are out of scope.

markers.unit: heterogeneous across labs: umol/L or arbitrary LC-MS/MS peak-area units as reported by source; not a standardized clinical assay
markers.why_new: No marker in the 60-item catalogue captures a blood NAD+ measurement; it is the direct pharmacodynamic readout of NMN and does not correspond to any existing marker. Attached to Cardiometabolic health because every trial that measured it also measured cardiometabolic endpoints (insulin sensitivity, lipids, blood pressure) in the same cohort, not because NAD+ itself is a cardiometabolic marker in other literature.

markers.name: Gait speed / walking function (4-m or 6-m walk time, stepping and chair-stand tests)
markers.unit: m/s or seconds per fixed distance; also 5-times-sit-to-stand time (s) as a lower-limb function proxy
markers.why_new: The catalogue's strength marker (max_strength) is 1RM/handgrip; NMN sarcopenia trials primarily report gait speed and chair-stand time as the functional-capacity outcome, which is a distinct construct worth keeping separate rather than folding into max_strength.

markers.name: Statin-associated muscle symptoms (pain, weakness, cramp, tiredness) and creatine kinase
markers.unit: pooled weighted mean difference on symptom rating scales as used per source trial (scale not uniformly named in the meta-analysis abstract, commonly a 0-10 VAS); creatine kinase in U/L as a separate sub-outcome
markers.why_new: No catalogue marker covers statin-drug-interaction muscle symptoms; attached to Cardiometabolic health because statin therapy and its side effects sit inside that goal's clinical context.

markers.name: Sperm parameters (concentration, motility, morphology, volume) and clinical pregnancy rate
markers.unit: concentration x10^6/mL, motility %, volume mL, morphology %, or odds ratio for clinical pregnancy, as reported by source
markers.why_new: No catalogue marker covers male fertility/sperm quality; attached to Male vitality as the nearest existing goal covering men's reproductive physiology, though that goal's stated definition (testosterone, vascular function, lean mass, libido) does not explicitly name fertility - flagged here rather than silently assumed.

edges.verbatim: Sleep restriction decreased the glucose disposal rate during the clamp (32.5 +/- 3.6 vs. 40.7 +/- 5.1 micromol x kg lean body mass(-1) x min(-1), P = 0009), reflecting decreased peripheral insulin sensitivity. Accordingly, sleep restriction decreased the rate of glucose infusion by approximately 25% (P = 0.001).
edges.key_results: Sleep restriction also increased endogenous glucose production during the clamp (4.4 vs 3.6 micromol/kg lean body mass/min, P=0.017), indicating hepatic (not just peripheral) insulin resistance, and raised plasma nonesterified fatty acid levels during the clamp (68 vs 57 micromol/L, P=0.005). This means a single bad night of sleep produces a measurable, gold-standard-confirmed reduction in insulin sensitivity across both liver and peripheral tissue, not merely a subjective or surrogate-marker effect.
edges.caveats: Very small sample (n=9), though the crossover design with each subject as their own control and the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp (the gold-standard insulin-sensitivity measure) partially offsets the small n. This is a single acute-exposure RCT, not a meta-analysis; a separate meta-analysis of 21 chronic sleep-restriction RCTs (Sondrup et al. 2022, DOI 10.1016/j.smrv.2022.101594) corroborates the direction (reduced insulin sensitivity by OGTT/IVGTT and HOMA-IR) but did not report a quantified pooled effect size in its abstract, so that corroborating paper could not itself be shipped as a quantified edge.
edges.review_note: This row was right on the screen and wrong underneath: it reports clamp glucose disposal, which FELL by about 25%, but recorded the direction as a rise and then inherited the HOMA-IR polarity where a rise is the harm. Two errors cancelled and the row showed the correct red. Recorded now as a fall on a measure where a rise is the benefit, which gives the same red for the reason the paper actually gives.

paper.title: Working Memory Training Does Not Improve Performance on Measures of Intelligence or Other Measures of 'Far Transfer': Evidence From a Meta-Analytic Review
paper.design: meta-analytic review of pretest-posttest controlled training studies

edges.verbatim: Immediately following training there were reliable improvements on measures of intermediate transfer (verbal and visuospatial working memory). For measures of far transfer (nonverbal ability, verbal ability, word decoding, reading comprehension, arithmetic) there was no convincing evidence of any reliable improvements when working memory training was compared with a treated control condition. Furthermore, mediation analyses indicated that across studies, the degree of improvement on working memory measures was not related to the magnitude of far-transfer effects found.
edges.key_results: Meta-analysis of 87 publications (145 experimental comparisons) of computerized working-memory ('brain') training programs using a pretest-posttest design with a control group. Training reliably improved performance on other (untrained) working-memory measures (near/intermediate transfer), but showed no convincing evidence of improvement on far-transfer measures such as nonverbal or verbal ability, reading, or arithmetic when compared against a treated control group. The amount of improvement on trained working-memory tasks did not predict the (absent) far-transfer benefit, and publication-bias analysis found no evidential value supporting far transfer across the literature. The authors conclude such programs produce short-term, task-specific effects that do not generalize to real-world cognitive skills.
edges.caveats: This is the canonical 'brain training doesn't transfer' null result central to this evidence tree: it directly contradicts marketing claims for commercial brain-training products; it does not evaluate every brain-training paradigm (e.g., action video games), only working-memory training specifically.

Multivitamin-mineral benefits were also observed for memory and executive function.
edges.key_results: COSMOS-Mind randomized 2,262 older adults (mean age 73) to daily multivitamin-mineral (MVM) supplementation or placebo for 3 years, assessing a global cognition composite (Telephone Interview of Cognitive Status, word list and story recall, oral trail-making, verbal fluency, number span, digit ordering) alongside memory and executive-function composites. Daily MVM produced a small but statistically significant benefit on global cognition, with a larger effect in participants with a cardiovascular disease history. Cocoa extract, tested in the same factorial design, had no effect on global cognition (mean z = 0.03; P = .28). Memory and executive function composites also improved with MVM.
edges.caveats: Effect size is small (z=0.07) though statistically significant; this is one of three COSMOS cognitive sub-studies and later pooled meta-analyses of all three report the effect as equivalent to about 2 years of reduced cognitive aging, a comparison not reproduced verbatim here since it was not in this trial's own abstract.

paper.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs

edges.verbatim: At six months, moderate-certainty evidence suggests that ginkgo probably has little to no effect on global clinical status measured on the Clinical Dementia Rating Scale (MD -0.03, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.01; 3 studies, 631 participants; I2 = 0%), cognition measured on the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale - cognition (MD -0.07, 95% CI -0.67 to 0.51; I2 = 0%; 2 studies, 508 participants), and ADLs measured on the Instrumental ADL scale (MD -0.05, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.19; 1 study, 350 participants).
edges.key_results: Updated Cochrane review (82 studies, 10,613 participants total across all populations) found that in people with mild cognitive impairment specifically, ginkgo versus placebo produced little to no effect at six months on global clinical status (Clinical Dementia Rating), cognition (ADAS-cog), or instrumental activities of daily living, all rated moderate-certainty evidence. In contrast, in people with diagnosed dementia the same review found small-to-moderate benefits on global status, cognition, and ADLs (low-certainty evidence). The authors conclude ginkgo probably has no benefit for MCI but may have small benefits once dementia is established.
edges.caveats: ADAS-cog comparison rests on only 2 studies / 508 participants; the review explicitly separates MCI (null) from dementia (small benefit) and from healthy/subjective-complaint populations (uncertain), so this edge should not be read as 'ginkgo does nothing for cognition' generally.

edges.verbatim: Each 1000 IU/day vitamin D3 supplementation slightly reduced depressive symptoms in individuals with and without depression (SMD: -0.32, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.22; GEADE = moderate). The effect was more pronounced in those with depressive symptoms (SMD: -0.57, 95% CI -0.69 to -0.44; n = 15). The greatest reduction occurred at 8000 IU/day (SMD: -2.04, 95% CI -3.77 to -0.31). Trials with follow-up ⩽8 weeks (SMD: -0.45, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.20; n = 8) and 8 to ⩽24 weeks (SMD: -0.47, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.24; n = 15) showed stronger effects compared to those lasting 24 to ⩽52 weeks (SMD: -0.13, 95% CI -0.28 to 0.02; n = 5) or longer than 52 weeks (SMD: 0.14, 95% CI -0.16 to 0.44; n = 3) (p group difference <0.001).
edges.key_results: This analysis included 31 trials with 24,189 participants. Each 1000 IU/day vitamin D3 supplementation slightly reduced depressive symptoms overall (SMD -0.32), more pronounced in those with depressive symptoms (SMD -0.57). Trials with follow-up of 24 weeks or less showed much stronger effects than longer trials, with the effect becoming non-significant by 24-52 weeks and reversing direction (non-significantly) beyond 52 weeks. This study suggests that vitamin D3 supplementation may effectively reduce depressive symptoms in the short term, but further high-quality trials are warranted for a conclusive long-term assessment.
edges.caveats: Effect size is strongly time-dependent and vanishes (then nominally reverses) with longer follow-up — a textbook case where reporting only the short-term headline number would overstate durable benefit; the 8000 IU/day 'greatest reduction' figure (-2.04) has a very wide CI (-3.77 to -0.31) suggesting a single or few small high-dose trials driving it, and is not used as this edge's primary number.

edges.caveats: This is the newer, bias-corrected side of a genuinely contested literature (see companion Stockwell 2016 edge below and the Millwood 2019 Mendelian randomisation edge under cardiovascular mortality). edges.key_results: A previous meta-analysis of the association between alcohol use and all-cause mortality found no statistically significant reductions in mortality risk at low levels of consumption compared with lifetime nondrinkers. Shown as a null, the row read as though alcohol does not affect mortality at all, which is the opposite of what the paper concludes. Recorded as a rise in mortality.

Genetic epidemiology shows that the apparently protective effects of moderate alcohol intake against stroke are largely non-causal. edges.verbatim: We found no significant association with consumption of 50 g/d RM using an empirical fit with lower consumption (relative risk [RR] 0.93 (0.8-1.02) or all consumption levels (1.04 (0.99-1.10)), while classical models showed RRs as high as 1.09 (1.00-1.18) at 50g/day.
edges.caveats: This paper is a methodological critique funded and authored by a risk-consulting firm (EpiX Analytics) whose broader client base includes food-industry-adjacent work; it does not claim red/processed meat is safe overall (it explicitly states a no-risk limit of 0 g/day is inconsistent with the evidence) but specifically challenges the standard dose-response modeling assumptions used to estimate risk at LOW consumption levels. Shipped alongside the Huang 2021 positive-association edge above rather than resolved into one number, per the task's requirement to record genuine model-dependence rather than picking a side.
edges.key_results: We found no significant association with consumption of 50 g/d red meat using an empirical fit with lower consumption (RR 0.93) or all consumption levels (1.04), while classical models showed RRs as high as 1.09 at 50 g/day. Processed meat consumption of 20 g/d was not associated with colorectal cancer (1.01) when using lower consumer data, regardless of model choice. Classical DRMA model assumptions and inclusion of higher consumption levels influence the association between colorectal cancer and low red and processed meat consumption. A no-risk limit of 0 g/d consumption of red meat and processed meat is inconsistent with the evidence.
edges.review_note: Higher intake, higher cancer risk. Unfavourable, correctly tagged.

paper.design: dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies

edges.verbatim: U-shaped associations were indicated between sleep duration and risk of all outcomes, with the lowest risk observed for ≈7-hour sleep duration per day, which was varied little by sex. For all-cause mortality, when sleep duration was <7 hours per day, the pooled relative risk (RR) was 1.06 (95% CI, 1.04-1.07) per 1-hour reduction; when sleep duration was >7 hours per day, the pooled RR was 1.13 (95% CI, 1.11-1.15) per 1-hour increment.
edges.caveats: Self-reported sleep duration in most included cohorts, which is an imprecise proxy for actual sleep; long sleep duration is itself frequently a marker of underlying illness, depression, or low socioeconomic status (reverse causation), which may explain part or all of the long-sleep side of the U-curve rather than long sleep directly causing harm.
edges.key_results: U-shaped associations were indicated between sleep duration and risk of all outcomes, with the lowest risk observed for approximately 7-hour sleep duration per day. For all-cause mortality, when sleep duration was less than 7 hours per day, the pooled RR was 1.06 per 1-hour reduction; when sleep duration was more than 7 hours per day, the pooled RR was 1.13 per 1-hour increment. Our findings indicate that both short and long sleep duration is associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events.

paper.design: meta-analytic review of prospective/longitudinal observational studies

edges.verbatim: Across studies in which several possible confounds were statistically controlled for, the weighted average effect sizes were as follows: social isolation odds ratio (OR) = 1.29, loneliness OR = 1.26, and living alone OR = 1.32, corresponding to an average of 29%, 26%, and 32% increased likelihood of mortality, respectively.
edges.caveats: Social connection cannot be randomized, so this is entirely observational; people who become isolated may already be in declining health (reverse causation) or share unmeasured traits (e.g., untreated depression, lower income) that independently raise mortality risk. edges.key_results: Actual and perceived social isolation are both associated with increased risk for early mortality. No differences were found between measures of objective and subjective social isolation. Overall, the influence of both objective and subjective social isolation on risk for mortality is comparable with well-established risk factors for mortality.

paper.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (2 case-control, 8 cross-sectional, 1 prospective cohort study pooled across outcomes)

edges.verbatim: The meta-analysis showed coffee consumption to be significantly associated with a 35% decreased odds of significant liver fibrosis (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.54-0.78, p < 0.00001).
edges.key_results: There was no heterogeneity for the fibrosis outcome (I2 = 11%, p = 0.34) and no evidence of publication bias (p = 0.134), unusually clean for an observational meta-analysis. Two earlier, smaller meta-analyses of overlapping literature found closely consistent effect sizes: Hayat et al. 2021 (RR 0.68) and Wijarnpreecha et al. 2017 (RR 0.70), both also reporting a significantly reduced risk of liver fibrosis in NAFLD patients who drink coffee. edges.caveats: All source studies are observational (mostly cross-sectional and case-control, one cohort); no RCT has tested coffee against liver fibrosis. Reverse causation (sicker patients avoiding coffee) and confounding by lifestyle (coffee drinkers differing systematically from non-drinkers) cannot be excluded by this design.

paper.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (dose-response and categorical)

edges.verbatim: In Japan, low alcohol consumption was consistently associated with substantially reduced incidence and prevalence of hepatic steatosis compared to non-drinkers (RR for <20g pure alcohol/day=0.75, 95% CI: 0.71-0.79, I(2)=0%). edges.key_results: Heterogeneity was essentially zero within Japan (I2=0%) but very high elsewhere (I2=84%), meaning the Japan finding is a stable and repeatable pattern while the null finding elsewhere reflects genuinely inconsistent studies rather than a single stable null. edges.caveats: This is a genuinely contested, unresolved finding rather than a simple protective or harmful effect - the population-dependence is itself the finding. All included studies are observational and cannot rule out a 'healthy drinker' confounding effect (light drinkers in some populations being healthier for unrelated reasons). Should not be read as evidence that alcohol is protective against fatty liver in general; the effect nulls out or reverses outside the specific Japanese cohorts studied.

paper.title: Xylitol-containing products for preventing dental caries in children and adults

edges.verbatim: The main finding of the review was that, over 2.5 to 3 years of use, a fluoride toothpaste containing 10% xylitol may reduce caries by 13% when compared to a fluoride-only toothpaste (PF -0.13, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.08, 4216 children analysed, low-quality evidence).
edges.key_results: The remaining evidence on children, from small single studies with risk of bias issues and great uncertainty associated with the effect estimates, was insufficient to determine a benefit from xylitol products. One study reported that xylitol syrup (8 g per day) reduced caries by 58% (95% CI 33% to 83%, 94 infants analysed, low quality evidence) when compared to a low-dose xylitol syrup (2.67 g per day) consumed for 1 year. The following results had 95% CIs that were compatible with both a reduction and an increase in caries associated with xylitol: xylitol lozenges versus no treatment in children; xylitol sucking tablets versus no treatment in infants; xylitol tablets versus control (sorbitol) tablets in infants; xylitol wipes versus control wipes in infants. There was only one study investigating the effects of xylitol lozenges, when compared to control lozenges, in adults; the effect estimate had a 95% CI that was compatible with both a reduction and an increase in caries associated with xylitol.
edges.caveats: CORRECTED FROM CANDIDATE 'xylitol chewing gum': this review does not isolate chewing gum as its own product category with a pooled effect estimate -- the abstract's only quantified positive finding concerns xylitol-containing toothpaste, and it is downgraded because it rests on two studies from a single author group in one population. Treat the popular claim that xylitol gum specifically prevents cavities as not established by this systematic review; direction is recorded as null (studied broadly, no reliable gum-specific effect identified) rather than as a confirmed benefit.
edges.review_note: This was marked as a null result. The review's own headline figure is a 13% reduction in caries with a confidence interval of -0.18 to -0.08, which excludes zero. It is a finding, not a null - a weak one, on low-quality evidence from two studies by one author group, which the row's own caveats already say. Recorded as a fall in caries.

cut.label: dairy_intake -> insulin_igf1 (milk raises circulating IGF-1)
cut.reason: A 2009 systematic review (Qin et al., Int J Food Sci Nutr, DOI 10.1080/09637480903150114) reports RCTs found a WMD of 13.8 ng/mL (95% CI 6.1-21.5) for IGF-1 in milk-intervention groups, and this number is corroborated by multiple independent secondary sources - but the primary abstract was paywalled/blocked from automated retrieval (PubMed cookie wall, ResearchGate/Tandfonline access denied), so no literal verbatim sentence could be obtained from the primary source. Per the acceptance bar, an edge without a verified verbatim sentence does not ship, even though the underlying claim is plausibly correct.

cut.label: sugar_reduction -> insulin_igf1
cut.reason: No dedicated RCT or meta-analysis was found that isolates generic 'sugar reduction' as a distinct exposure from glycemic-load/carbohydrate modification (which is already captured by the low_gi_diet edges) or from fructose specifically (which has its own, narrower literature on hepatic vs peripheral insulin resistance). Treating it as a separate edge risked double-counting the low-GI diet finding under a different label or fabricating precision the literature does not support.

cut.label: curcumin phytosome (Meriva) -> hs_crp_il6, quantified
cut.reason: Multiple RCTs (e.g., Meriva-brand phytosomal curcumin trials) qualitatively report larger CRP reductions than unformulated curcumin, but no verbatim, quantified pooled result sentence could be retrieved within the research budget for this specific formulation as its own meta-analysis. The curcumin_piperine edges above already demonstrate formulation-dependence; phytosome-specific numbers are flagged as an open item rather than asserted from search-summary text alone.

cut.label: alcohol -> hs_crp_il6 (added candidate, not in original list)
cut.reason: Design spec section 4.2 flags alcohol as a high-leverage cross-tree behavior worth adding, but the CRP relationship in the literature is J/U-shaped (moderate intake associated with lower CRP than both abstention and heavy intake) and the evidence base is cross-sectional/cohort, not RCT (ethically, heavy drinking cannot be randomized long-term). The schema's single-direction (+/-/null) field cannot faithfully represent a non-monotonic dose-response without misleading simplification, so this was left out of Goal B rather than forced into a binary direction. Better suited to Goal C (sleep) where the REM-suppression literature is more directly dose-linear, if pursued separately.

cut.label: Ambient room temperature -> Sleep onset latency
cut.reason: Could not obtain a verbatim, numerically-quantified result sentence from a resolvable-DOI primary source directly linking ambient/bedroom temperature to sleep onset latency in minutes. The one systematic review located with a clean DOI (Bennett et al. 2024, Sleep Medicine Reviews, DOI 10.1016/j.smrv.2024.101915, 'A systematic review of ambient heat and sleep in a warming climate') confirms only a directional association ('higher outdoor or indoor temperatures are generally associated with degraded sleep quality and quantity') with no minute-level quantification in its abstract. Other specific numeric claims surfaced during search (e.g. '5C increase -> ~2 min SOL increase', '+0.04 min per degF from 3.75 million nights') traced only to secondary AI-generated summaries or an unpublished conference abstract (SLEEP supplement) without a verifiable, resolvable-DOI verbatim sentence backing the exact number. Per the no-assertion-from-memory rule, this edge is cut rather than shipped with an unverifiable number.

cut.label: coffee consumption -> LDL cholesterol, precisely quantified pooled effect size
cut.reason: The one available RCT meta-analysis (Jee et al. 2001, DOI 10.1093/aje/153.4.353) establishes a clear dose-response direction (unfiltered coffee raises LDL, filtered does not) but its abstract does not report a numeric pooled effect size, and the full text was not retrievable within the research budget. Shipped as a qualitative edge instead (direction with no numeric effect) rather than cut outright, per the rule that a qualitative, directionally-supported finding is acceptable when no number is available to misstate.

cut.label: aerobic exercise -> resting heart rate (quantified reduction), as its own dedicated edge
cut.reason: Training-induced bradycardia is well established physiologically, but the specific meta-analyses located within budget either did not report a clean pooled resting-HR number (a 2026 detraining meta-analysis reported resting HR as 'no longer significant' in the reversal/detraining direction, not the training direction) or were not accessed in time. The resting_hr_arterial_stiffness marker slot is instead filled by the sauna null-result edge; a dedicated quantified aerobic-exercise-to-resting-HR edge is a good candidate for a follow-up research pass.

cut.label: sleep duration (habitual, non-experimental) -> HbA1c/fasting glucose, dose-response meta-analysis
cut.reason: Multiple cohort studies link short habitual sleep to higher diabetes risk, but a quantified RCT or meta-analysis giving a specific HbA1c or fasting-glucose number tied to a specific sleep-duration change (rather than diabetes incidence risk ratios) was not located within the research budget. The sleep_restriction -> insulin_sensitivity_homa_ir edge (Donga 2010) covers the same underlying mechanism with a single well-controlled RCT instead.

cut.label: resistance training -> HbA1c / insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes
cut.reason: Multiple recent (2026) meta-analyses on this topic were identified in PubMed search results but not fetched and reviewed within the research budget after the edge list reached sufficient breadth across all seven target markers with aerobic exercise, weight loss, Mediterranean diet, and sleep restriction already covering the glycemic/insulin-sensitivity markers. Worth a follow-up pass given resistance training's inclusion in the confirmed behavior list.

cut.label: HIIT -> blood pressure, as a chronic training effect distinct from VO2max
cut.reason: HIIT is confirmed and well evidenced for VO2max (shipped above) but a dedicated chronic HIIT-training blood-pressure meta-analysis distinct from acute post-exercise hypotension studies was not located and fetched within the research budget; the blood_pressure marker is already well covered by aerobic exercise, resistance training, DASH, sodium reduction, alcohol reduction, and added sugar.

cut.label: vitamin D / zinc / magnesium supplementation -> any cardiometabolic marker
cut.reason: These behaviors belong to the Goal A (male vitality) and Goal C (sleep) candidate lists per the design spec's section 4.1, not the cardiometabolic marker set specified for this file, so no search was performed for them here.

cut.label: protein_intake -> lean_mass, distribution/timing across the day (e.g., 4x25g pattern) as its own behavior
cut.reason: No dedicated, adequately powered RCT or meta-analysis was found within the research budget that isolates meal-to-meal protein distribution as a body-composition outcome separable from total daily protein intake; the existing distribution literature (e.g., Areta et al. 2013) measures acute muscle protein synthesis, not fat mass/lean mass/strength changes over weeks-to-months, so it does not meet this project's outcome bar. Folded into the protein_intake behavior's dose_or_intensity field instead of a separate node.

cut.label: hmb -> lean_mass, older/sarcopenic adults (as a second, separate edge)
cut.reason: Multiple 2024-2025 meta-analyses (e.g. PMC12655442, PMC12003145) report modest/mixed effects of HMB on handgrip strength and physical-performance batteries in adults over 50, but conflicting reviews and no single verbatim-quotable pooled estimate specifically for appendicular or total lean mass was retrieved within the research budget for this pass; left out rather than asserted from search-summary text alone.
